original_value: This paper presents a rotating focused field eddy-current (EC) sensing technique, which leverages the advantages of magnetic field focusing and rotating magnetic field, for arbitrary orientation defects detection. The sensor consists of four identical excitation coils orthogonally arranged in an upside-down pyramid configuration and a giant magneto-resistive (GMR) detection element. The four coils are connected to form two figure-8-shaped focusing sub-probes, which are fed by two identical harmonic currents with 90 degrees phase difference. A finite element model-based study of arbitrary orientation defects detection was performed to understand the probe operational characteristics and optimize its design parameters. Probe prototyping and experimental validation were also carried out on a carbon steel plate specimen with four prefabricated surface-breaking defects. In-situ spot inspection with the probe rotating above the defect and a manual line-scan inspection were both conducted. Results showed that the probe has the capability of detecting defects with any orientations while maintaining the same sensitivity and the defect depth can be quantitatively evaluated by using the signal amplitude. Compared with the existing rotating field probes, the presented probe does not require additional excitation adjustment or data fusion. Meanwhile, due to its focusing effect, it can generate a strong rotating magnetic field at the defect location with a weak background noise, thus yielding superior signal-to-noise ratio.

result.paraphrase: This paper proposes a rotating focused-field eddy-current (EC) sensing method that combines magnetic-field focusing with a rotating magnetic field to detect defects of arbitrary orientation. The sensor includes four identical excitation coils arranged orthogonally in an upside-down pyramid and a giant magneto-resistive (GMR) sensing element. These four coils are wired into two figure-8 focusing sub-probes, driven by two identical harmonic currents with a 90-degree phase difference. A finite-element-model study was conducted to analyze arbitrary-orientation defect detection and optimize the probe’s design parameters. The probe was then prototyped and experimentally validated on a carbon-steel plate specimen containing four prefabricated surface-breaking defects. Both in-situ spot inspection, with the probe rotating above the defect, and manual line-scan inspection were performed. The results showed that the probe can detect defects of any orientation with the same sensitivity, and defect depth can be quantitatively assessed from the signal amplitude. Compared with existing rotating-field probes, the proposed design requires no extra excitation adjustment or data fusion. In addition, its focusing effect produces a strong rotating magnetic field at the defect location while keeping background noise low, resulting in a superior signal-to-noise ratio.
